records.title: Cross-Contract Reentrancy Detection via Multi-Hop Call-Graph Traversal (CP-121)
records.body:
### Problem Statement
ChainProof's existing reentrancy detectors (`CP-107`, `swc107-reentrancy-v2.ts`) analyze external-call-before-state-update patterns within a single function/contract. The multi-file import-graph and call-graph resolution built for the "Multi-file contract analysis with inheritance and import graph resolution" work gives ChainProof the infrastructure to see across contract boundaries, but no rule currently uses it to detect **cross-contract reentrancy**: the case where Contract A calls into Contract B, which calls back into Contract A (directly, or via a third Contract C), re-entering a function whose state hasn't been finalized yet. This is precisely the pattern behind several real-world exploits in vault/strategy architectures and is invisible to single-function analysis.

### Proposed Solution
Implement a new detector, `CP-121` (multi-hop cross-contract reentrancy), built on top of the existing `rules/call-graph.ts` infrastructure:

- Traverse the resolved call graph across the full set of scanned and imported contracts to find call chains of length two or more (`A.f() → B.g() → A.h()`, or longer) where the re-entered contract (`A`) has unfinalized state changes pending between the initial external call and the point of re-entry.
- Distinguish chains that are protected by a consistent reentrancy guard (e.g., a `nonReentrant`-style modifier applied across the whole chain, or checks-effects-interactions correctly applied at every hop) from genuinely exploitable chains.
- Support a configurable traversal depth (default 3 hops) with a hard cap to keep analysis time bounded on large protocols, and short-circuit cycles that don't involve unfinalized state.
- Findings must reference the full call chain (each contract/function/line in the path), not just the terminal re-entrant call, so the report is actionable.
- Integrate with the existing severity model (`critical`, given this class of bug is typically fund-draining) and with the Slither merge/deduplication logic so a Slither-detected same-chain finding doesn't produce a duplicate.

### Technical Scope
- New `packages/core/src/rules/cp121-cross-contract-reentrancy.ts` implementing the traversal and detection logic against the existing `CallGraph` type from `rules/call-graph.ts`.
- Extend `rules/rule-context.ts` if needed so the rule has access to the full multi-file call graph, not just the current file's AST.
- Register the rule in `scanner.ts` and add it to the vulnerability rules table in the README.
- New fixture contracts under `examples/contracts/` demonstrating a 2-hop and a 3-hop exploitable cross-contract reentrancy, plus a correctly guarded (non-vulnerable) equivalent for false-positive testing.
- Unit tests covering: direct 2-hop reentrancy, 3-hop reentrancy through an intermediate contract, correctly guarded chains producing no finding, and a depth-limited case that should not be flagged beyond the configured maximum hops.

### Acceptance Criteria
- Detects the 2-hop and 3-hop fixture exploits with the full call chain reported in the finding.
- Does not flag the guarded fixture (zero false positives on that case).
- Analysis time on the existing `examples/` fixture set stays within the current scan performance budget (no more than a small, documented constant-factor slowdown).
- The new rule appears in the README's Vulnerability Rules table with its SWC cross-reference where applicable.

### Estimated Scope
Approximately 700 lines of new TypeScript across the rule, fixtures, and tests.


---
<!-- maintainer-scope-upgrade-2026-08 -->

This issue is being expanded into a substantial, production-quality ChainProof enhancement. The implementation should be designed as maintainable platform work, not as a narrow proof of concept. ### Expanded Objective

Implement CP-121 as a multi-hop, cross-contract reentrancy detector using resolved import and call-graph context. The feature should fit the existing monorepo architecture, reuse current scanner/report/CLI patterns where appropriate, and avoid introducing ad hoc subsystems that are difficult to test or maintain.

records.title: Record durable extraction runs and proposition run lineage
records.body:
## Goal

Record durable, tenant-scoped extraction runs and link propositions to every run that
produced or confirmed them without changing source-grounding cardinality.

## Context

Projection and collector runs establish the DICE storage pattern. Extraction needs its
own lifecycle, metadata envelope, indexes, parent/superseded links, and a dedicated
proposition-to-run relation. `ProvenanceEntry` and `DerivedFrom` remain source evidence.

A run may contain zero, one, or many model invocations because of chunking or retries.
Requested configuration, observed execution facts, optional provider-effective facts,
and protected replay evidence must remain distinct.

The design borrows the separation of run/job/input/output from OpenLineage, the
parameters/metrics/context/artifact split from MLflow, requested-versus-response model
facts and opt-in content from OpenTelemetry GenAI, and #64's S3/W3C-PROV-style stable
source plus opaque revision. It uses typed fields rather than generic facet/tag maps.

The resulting evidence supports troubleshooting failures, comparing and evaluating runs,
approximate reproduction, auditing proposition output, and investigating user-context
effects. Experiment/user-context comparisons use tenant-scoped run pages and host-side
grouping; they do not imply new push-down filters or REST endpoints.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ExtractionRun` records tenant, profile, ordered source revisions, pass, parent/
      superseded lineage, experiment/cohort, prompt/template and schema fingerprints,
      metamodel, extractor/host/runtime, status, timing, counts, and bounded failures.
- [ ] Requested model configuration records portable model/role, temperature, penalties,
      max tokens, top-k/top-p, thinking/selection fingerprints, and timeout without
      serializing provider extension objects.
- [ ] Repeatable invocation records capture only genuinely observed configured service,
      usage, timing, attempt, outcome, and optional provider-response facts.
- [ ] Opaque actor, request, session, personalization, and deployment references support
      audit without retaining PII or arbitrary user-context maps.
- [ ] Raw prompt/source/user-context payloads are absent by default; optional replay
      material is represented only by classified, expiring protected-content references.
- [ ] Replay fidelity is explicit and never promises exact deterministic replay.
- [ ] DICE ships scoped in-memory and Drivine stores, indexes, schema registration,
      lifecycle coordination, invocation correlation, and autoconfiguration.
- [ ] Empty, completed, failed, and cancelled headers persist; retries are idempotent and
      incompatible terminal rewrites are rejected.
- [ ] Proposition-to-run is dedicated many-to-many attribution using canonical saved ids.
- [ ] Parent and superseded chains are axis-explicit, bounded, cycle-safe, and queryable.
- [ ] Repository, authorized REST, and bundle lineage expose run refs separately from sources.
- [ ] Two identical-content runs produce one proposition/source grounding and two run links.
- [ ] Every lookup, join, inverse query, chain, page, and aggregate fails closed across tenants.
- [ ] Legacy callers, Java descriptors, existing `/why` JSON, and hosts without configured
      run storage retain current behavior.

## Constraints

- Do not add run identity to source-provenance equality.
- Depends on #64's final source-revision contract and #66's profile/current-run refs.
- Do not guess provider-effective values from requested configuration.
- Do not persist credentials, raw prompts/source text, full user/session objects, provider
  SDK responses, native usage objects, or arbitrary extension maps.
- Follow current collector/projection store conventions.
- Land through a reviewed PR to `main`. PR #71 completed the Spring/Embabel upgrade;
  the operator confirmed `main` is the sole delivery target and no backport is required.

## Out of scope

- Atomic product commit.
- Product batching and later-pass orchestration.
- Host replay policy or exact replay guarantees.
- Encrypted blob storage, KMS, retention scheduling, authentication, or actor-directory ownership.

## Original request

Record which model, prompt, schema, profile, source revisions, runtime, user/request
context, and observed execution conditions produced knowledge so extraction incidents,
evaluation, cost, drift, testing, and re-analysis are auditable.

records.title: ACL parent cycle causes infinite recursion in BasicLookupStrategy.convert()
records.body:
`AclImpl.setParent()` only rejects direct self-parenting (`newParent.equals(this)`); it does not detect indirect cycles (A → B → A, or longer chains). Once such a cycle is persisted via `JdbcMutableAclService.updateAcl()`, every subsequent lookup of any ACL in the cycle recurses forever.

**Where:**
- `AclImpl.setParent(Acl)` (`acl/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/acls/domain/AclImpl.java`) only guards `newParent.equals(this)` — no ancestor walk.
- `JdbcMutableAclService.updateObjectIdentity(MutableAcl)` (`acl/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/acls/jdbc/JdbcMutableAclService.java`) writes `parentId` with no cycle check.
- `BasicLookupStrategy.convert(...)` (`acl/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/acls/jdbc/BasicLookupStrategy.java`, ~lines 386-431) recurses on `StubAclParent` ids with no visited-set, so a stored cycle causes unconditional infinite recursion / `StackOverflowError` on every future read. `JdbcMutableAclService.clearCacheIncludingChildren(...)` has the same unguarded recursive shape.

**Repro sketch:**
1. User owns (or has `CHANGE_GENERAL` on) two ACL-protected objects A and B.
2. `aclA.setParent(aclB); aclService.updateAcl(aclA);`
3. `aclB.setParent(aclA); aclService.updateAcl(aclB);`
4. Any subsequent `aclService.readAclById(...)` for A or B recurses forever.

**Suggested fix shape:**
- In `AclImpl.setParent(Acl)`, walk `newParent`'s ancestor chain via `getParentAcl()` and reject (`IllegalArgumentException`, same unchecked pattern as the existing self-parent `Assert.isTrue`) if `this` is reachable.
- In `JdbcMutableAclService.updateObjectIdentity(MutableAcl)`, walk the proposed parent's stored ancestry before writing `parentId` and reject on a match, for the case where the in-memory check is bypassed (e.g. a custom `MutableAcl` implementation, or direct DB manipulation).
- Add a visited-`Set` guard in `BasicLookupStrategy.convert(...)` and `clearCacheIncludingChildren(...)` so that already-corrupt data (e.g. from before this fix, or written through a path that skips the new checks) fails fast with a clear exception instead of a `StackOverflowError`.

This should be additive/non-breaking: a stored parent cycle is already guaranteed to crash every future read of the affected ACLs, so no working application depends on being able to create one. Rejecting the write earlier, with a clear exception, doesn't remove any capability that currently functions.

records.title: DM-55388: Intersphinx-based link domains for the Ook Links API
records.body:
### Jira Key

DM-55388

### Jira URL

https://rubinobs.atlassian.net/browse/DM-55388

### Summary

Extend Ook's Links API (SQR-086) beyond the SDM domain with link domains seeded from Sphinx intersphinx object inventories, starting with a Python API domain at `/links/domains/python`. Ook pulls `objects.inv` files on a schedule through the DM-55387 intersphinx inventory cache (ook#236, a prerequisite) from a new registry of documentation sites, stores entries in a generic hierarchical entity table, and serves per-object documentation deep links (e.g. for `lsst.afw.table.SourceCatalog`).

### Scope

In scope:

- **Generic intersphinx entity storage** (Alembic migration + schema dump update):
  - `intersphinx_entity` table — identity `(sphinx_domain, name)`; columns `role`, `dispname`, nullable self-referential `parent_id`, and a JSONB `extras` column (the escape hatch for later SDM convergence). Hierarchy is computed at ingest by per-Sphinx-domain naming strategies (for `py`: dotted-name splitting, parent resolved by name lookup).
  - `links_intersphinx` join table — a new polymorphic `SqlLink` subtype (`polymorphic_identity="intersphinx"`) with FKs to both `intersphinx_entity` and `intersphinx_source`; the source FK enables per-source replace/prune.
- **Source registry**:
  - `intersphinx_source` table — inventory URL, human title (surfaces as link `collection_title`), enabled flag, and observability columns (`last_ingested_at`, `last_status`, `last_error`).
  - CRUD API at `/ook/intersphinx/sources`; writes gated by an admin scope (`exec:admin`), not the `write:intersphinx` cache-warming scope.
- **Ingest pipeline (pull model)**:
  - `IntersphinxIngestService` under `services/ingest/`: iterate enabled sources, fetch each inventory through the DM-55387 cache service, parse with `sphobjinv` (new dependency), filter to the `py` Sphinx domain for the MVP, derive hierarchy, and replace that source's links atomically in a per-site transaction.
  - Stale-data policy: full replace per source on each ingest; entities left with no links from any source and no link-holding descendants are pruned.
  - Failure policy: a fetch/parse failure on one source is logged and stamped on its registry row (its previous links are kept) and the run continues with remaining sources; the CLI exits non-zero if any source failed so the CronJob shows red.
  - Triggers: new `ook ingest-intersphinx` CLI command (run by a Kubernetes CronJob, matching the `ook refresh-intersphinx` pattern) and `POST /ingest/intersphinx` (admin; accepts an optional source URL to ingest a single source).
  - The service is structured so a future Kafka consumer (Docverse publish events, once restored) can trigger the same per-source ingest path.
- **Links API surface**:
  - `GET /links/domains/python` — domain info endpoint (mirroring the SDM one).
  - `GET /links/domains/python/objects` — paginated collection of entities with their links (Safir keyset cursors, `X-Total-Count`).
  - `GET /links/domains/python/objects/{name}` — links for one object; identity is the fully qualified name.
  - `GET /links/domains/python/objects/{name}/children` — paginated listing of direct children (a module's classes/functions, a class's methods) with their links.
  - `GET /links/domains` — new cross-domain index listing available domains (`sdm`, `python`) with their entity/collection URL templates, generalizing `SdmDomainInfo`.
- Only the canonical/default version of each documentation site is ingested (one inventory URL per registry row; no version dimension in the schema).
- **SDM-convergence design note**: a written design under `planning/` mapping SDM's per-entity tables onto the generic entity model (typed TAP sort keys → `extras` JSONB, pagination-cursor ordering, Felis IDs), to seed a follow-up PRD. The migration itself does not land here.
- **Tests** (all four tiers pinned as acceptance criteria):
  - Parser + hierarchy strategy: unit tests with fixture `objects.inv` files, including a real pipelines.lsst.io sample (parse correctness, dotted-name parent derivation, missing-parent and `$`-suffix URI edge cases).
  - Store layer: testcontainers-Postgres integration tests (per-source replace, orphan pruning, recursive-CTE children queries, cursor pagination).
  - Ingest service: end-to-end against a mocked cache/HTTP layer (per-site transaction, failure record-and-continue, idempotent re-ingest).
  - API endpoints: python-domain routes, domains index, sources CRUD auth, manual ingest trigger.

Out of scope:

- Documenteer changes — none are required under the pull-via-cache model; client-side intersphinx work is already covered by documenteer#318 (DM-55387).
- Phalanx work — CronJob manifest, ingress scope config, token distribution (consistent with the DM-55387 PRD pair).
- Migrating the SDM domain onto the generic entity table (follow-up PRD; only the design note lands here).
- Sphinx domains beyond `py`, multi-version ingest, push-based ingest, and the Kafka trigger itse

records.title: Test -creating a impact analysis agent
records.body:
## Elaborated Requirement

**Issue:** #3 — Impact Analysis Agent for PR Merges
**Type:** Story
**Verdict:** `NEEDS CLARIFICATION`

---

### Summary

A developer or tech lead wants an AI-powered agent that automatically analyses the downstream impact of merging a pull request into the project. The underlying intent is to reduce the cognitive load on reviewers who must manually trace how a change propagates across the codebase — catching breaking changes, affected modules, and risky dependencies before they reach production. Success is defined as the agent surfacing a concise, accurate impact report at PR merge time that reduces post-merge incidents caused by overlooked side effects. This fits naturally alongside the existing PR Review Agent (which focuses on code quality) and the Requirement Analysis Agent (which focuses on intent alignment), forming a third pillar of automated engineering guardrails in this platform.

| Dimension | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Stated need** | An agent that identifies the impact when merging a PR to the project |
| **Underlying intent** | Prevent unintended side effects from reaching production by surfacing affected areas automatically, without the reviewer needing to manually trace dependencies |
| **Success definition** | Reviewer receives a clear impact report (affected modules, risk level, potential breakage) before or at the point of merge, enabling a confident go/no-go decision |
| **Current workaround** | Reviewers manually inspect changed files, cross-reference callers, and rely on test suite coverage — a slow, error-prone, and experience-dependent process |

---

### User Context & Workflow

- **Who & when:** Primarily a developer or tech lead reviewing a PR under time pressure; also useful for an author self-reviewing before requesting review. Context is typically high-stress: release windows, sprint deadlines, or incident hotfixes where the cost of a missed side effect is high.
- **Constraints:** Must integrate non-intrusively into the existing PR workflow (GitHub webhook or PR comment trigger); output must be scannable in under 60 seconds; must not block the merge process — advisory only unless configured otherwise.
- **Workflow:**
  1. A PR is opened or updated against the main/target branch
  2. The impact analysis agent is triggered (via webhook, GitHub Action, or PR comment command)
  3. Agent analyses the diff — changed files, functions, interfaces, data contracts
  4. Agent traces call graphs, module dependencies, and shared data structures to identify affected areas
  5. Agent posts a structured impact report as a PR comment (e.g., affected modules, risk rating, suggested areas to test)
  6. Reviewer reads the report alongside the PR Review Agent output and makes a merge decision
- **Decision points:** Whether to block merge on high-risk impact (human decision vs automated gate); which branches/environments are in scope; whether to include test coverage gap analysis as part of the impact report.

---

### Domain Context

- **Key concepts:**
  - *Impact* in this context means: which other modules, services, APIs, consumers, or data flows are likely to be affected by the changed code — not just what files changed, but what depends on those files.
  - *PR merge impact* differs from static analysis: it is relational (dependency graph traversal) rather than just syntactic.
- **Business rules:**
  - Impact should be assessed relative to the target branch (not just the PR branch in isolation).
  - Indirect dependencies (e.g., A calls B, B calls C — a change to C affects A) should be surfaced, ideally up to a configurable depth.
  - The report should distinguish between *confirmed* impact (direct callers changed) and *potential* impact (indirect or inferred).
- **User expectations:** Fast enough to complete before a reviewer finishes reading the diff (target: under 2 minutes); trustworthy enough that a false negative (missed impact) is rare; simple enough that the report requires no interpretation.
- **Competitive/industry patterns:**
  - GitHub's own Copilot PR summaries provide diff summaries but do not perform dependency-level impact tracing.
  - Tools like Codecov, SonarQube, and Nx affected graph analysis are adjacent but narrower (test coverage gaps or monorepo task graphs respectively).
  - Commercial tools like Moderne, Sourcegraph, and CodeScene offer call-graph analysis; the differentiator here is tight integration with the existing xianix agent platform and its GitHub webhook pipeline.
  - The PR Review Agent in this repo already indexes the codebase before review — this agent can reuse that index as a dependency graph input, avoiding duplicate work.

---

### Gaps & Unresolved Questions

| # | Gap / Question | Severity | Suggested question |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Scope of "impact" is undefined — does it mean module/file dependencies, API contract changes, database schema effects, or all of the above? | `CRITICAL` | What types of impact are in scope for the

records.title: feat: add deterministic symbol and dependency graph queries
records.body:
## Objective

Expose deterministic structural navigation over the live commit so agents can trace definitions, references, dependencies, call paths, inheritance, and change impact without repeatedly reading whole files.

## Scope

- Implement or adapt Tree-sitter/LSP-backed symbol, definition/reference, import, inheritance, caller/callee, route, and test-association queries where language support permits.
- Return compact paths and cited nodes/edges before source bodies.
- Preserve provider/language confidence and distinguish parsed, inferred, unresolved, and dynamic relationships.
- Support bounded traversal depth, cycle handling, fan-out limits, and explicit truncation.
- Validate every structural result against the commit-scoped snapshot before use.
- Fall back to exact local exploration when a language, edge type, or dynamic construct is unsupported.

## Acceptance criteria

- Conformance fixtures cover supported languages, cross-file calls/imports, inheritance, cycles, overloads, dynamic dispatch, and unresolved edges.
- Every node and edge has resolvable provenance and snapshot identity.
- Impact and call-path queries remain within result/token/latency limits and report truncation.
- Unsupported or low-confidence relationships are never presented as authoritative facts.
- Benchmarks compare structural queries against the current grep/read baseline.

## Dependencies

- #806
- #807

records.title: Datalog et graph queries — l'alternative SQL méconnue
records.body:
---
lede: Datalog est un langage de query déclaratif qui excelle là où SQL souffre : relations récursives, transitive closure, graph traversal. XTDB, Datomic, Datascript le rendent accessible.
lede_en: Datalog is a declarative query language excelling where SQL struggles: recursive relations, transitive closure, graph traversal. XTDB, Datomic, Datascript make it accessible.
title_en: Datalog and graph queries — the underrated SQL alternative
---

<!--lang:fr-->

## Pourquoi connaître Datalog

SQL est puissant mais souffre sur certaines requêtes :

- **Transitive closure** (qui est ancêtre de qui, qui suit qui directement ou indirectement) : nécessite `WITH RECURSIVE` complexe.
- **Graph traversal** : multi-hops, friend-of-friend, shortest path — SQL devient illisible.
- **Time-travel queries** : "qui était assigné à ce ticket il y a 3 mois ?" — partition par date manuelle.

Datalog résout ces cas naturellement, avec une syntaxe déclarative plus simple.

## Le concept

Datalog s'inspire de Prolog. Vous écrivez des **règles** (faits + dérivations) et des **queries**.

```clojure
;; Datalog (syntaxe EDN, Datomic-style)
;; Trouver tous les ancêtres de Khalil

[:find ?ancestor
 :where
 [?khalil :person/name "Khalil"]
 [?khalil :person/parent ?ancestor]]

;; Récursif : tous les ancêtres directs et indirects
[:find ?ancestor
 :where
 [?khalil :person/name "Khalil"]
 (ancestor ?khalil ?ancestor)]

;; Rule definition
(rule ancestor [?person ?ancestor]
  ((or [?person :person/parent ?ancestor]
       (and [?person :person/parent ?intermediate]
            (ancestor ?intermediate ?ancestor)))))
```

La rule récursive est triviale. En SQL, vous écrivez du `WITH RECURSIVE` de 20 lignes.

## Where it excels

- **Recursive queries** : ancêtres, descendants, hierarchies illimitées.
- **Graph patterns** : matching de sous-graphes complexes.
- **Transitive relations** : "tous les users connectés à X par n'importe quelle chaîne d'amitiés".
- **Audit / time-travel** : Datomic stocke immutable history, queries "as of t" naturelles.

## Les implémentations modernes

**XTDB** :

- Open source, écrit en Clojure.
- Time-travel queries natives.
- Pluggable storage (RocksDB, Kafka, JDBC).
- API HTTP standard.

**Datomic** :

- Commercial (Cognitect, Nubank).
- Production-grade, utilisé par Walmart, plusieurs banques.
- Modèle économique : queries gratuites (sur peer JVM), writes payants.

**Datascript** :

- Datalog dans le navigateur (ClojureScript).
- État local d'apps React-like reactive en datalog.
- Sweet spot : Roam Research, Logseq.

**Datalevin** :

- Open source, embedded, écrit en Clojure.
- Alternative à SQLite pour des apps avec relations complexes.

## Cas d'usage 2026

- **Knowledge graphs** : Roam Research, Logseq, Obsidian — tous datalog underneath.
- **Apps d'analyse réseau** : qui est connecté à qui, influencer maps.
- **Génétique / biotechnologie** : relations dans des graphes biologiques.
- **Compliance & audit** : "qui a touché à ce record et quand ?" — datalog time-travel.

## Vs Cypher (Neo4j)

Neo4j utilise **Cypher**, un autre langage de graph query. Différences :

- **Cypher** : optimisé pour les graphes, ASCII-art syntax pour les paths.
- **Datalog** : plus général, peut aussi faire du relationnel pur.

```cypher
// Cypher
MATCH (k:Person {name: 'Khalil'})-[:PARENT*]->(ancestor)
RETURN ancestor
```

Cypher reste plus populaire pour graph databases pures. Datalog brille pour les apps mixant relationnel + graph + history.

## Limites

- **Talent pool** : encore plus restreint que SQL. Recrutement difficile.
- **Tooling** : SQL a 50 ans d'écosystème. Datalog a moins de tutoriels, moins d'IDE support.
- **Performance** : sur des queries simples, SQL souvent plus rapide grâce à des décennies d'optimisations.

## Apprendre Datalog

- **Learn Datalog Today** (gratuit en ligne) : cours interactif court.
- **Datascript playground** : essayer dans le browser.
- **Building a Datomic app** tutoriels.

Apprendre Datalog en 1 weekend rend meilleur en SQL aussi — vous comprenez différemment les relations.

## Verdict

Pour 95 % des projets : SQL reste le bon choix. Pour des apps spécifiques avec graph traversal, time-travel, ou knowledge management : Datalog mérite un essai.

Comme Common Lisp : pas mainstream, mais ceux qui l'utilisent ne reviennent rarement à SQL pur. Investissement intellectuel qui paye.

<!--/lang:fr-->

## Why know Datalog

SQL is powerful but suffers on some queries:

- **Transitive closure** (who's ancestor of whom, who follows directly or indirectly): needs complex `WITH RECURSIVE`.

Datalog handles these naturally, with a simpler declarative syntax.

records.title: Syllabus of Competitive Pr0graming
records.body:
**1. Introduction to Programming Languages and Basics:**

Choose a programming language (e.g., C++, Python, Java) and become proficient in it.
Learn the basics of your chosen language, including data types, loops, conditionals, and I/O operations.

**2. Time Complexity and Big O Notation:**

Understand the concept of time complexity.
Learn how to analyze the time complexity of algorithms using Big O notation.

**3. Basic Data Structures:**

Arrays
Strings
Linked Lists
Stacks
Queues

**4. Elementary Algorithms:**

Sorting algorithms (e.g., Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, Merge Sort, Quick Sort)
Searching algorithms (e.g., Linear Search, Binary Search)

**5. Recursion and Backtracking:**

Understand recursive algorithms.
Learn backtracking techniques for solving problems with decision trees.

**6. Advanced Data Structures:**

Trees (Binary Trees, Binary Search Trees, AVL Trees, Heaps)
Graphs (Adjacency Matrix, Adjacency List)
Hashing (Hash Tables)

**7. Dynamic Programming:**

Master the concept of dynamic programming.
Solve classic DP problems (e.g., Fibonacci, Coin Change, Longest Common Subsequence).

**8. Greedy Algorithms:**

Learn the greedy strategy.
Solve problems that can be optimized using greedy algorithms.

**9. Graph Algorithms:**

Breadth-First Search (BFS)
Depth-First Search (DFS)
Shortest Path Algorithms (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford)
Minimum Spanning Tree (Prim's, Kruskal's)
Topological Sorting

**10. Advanced Algorithms:**

records.title: Hard `delete_comment` under-counts when a reply's parent is on a different record
records.body:
Follow-up from #2261 (`#[commentable]`, closes #1367). Raised by Codex review.

## The problem

With `soft_delete = false`, `delete_comment` gathers the descendant closure with a recursive CTE **scoped to one record** (`commentable_id = $parent`), then issues `DELETE FROM comments WHERE id IN (…)` and applies a counter delta of `ids.len()`.

If a comment on record **B** has `parent_id` pointing at a comment on record **A**, the CTE correctly excludes B's row — but the generated `parent_id … REFERENCES comments(id) ON DELETE CASCADE` removes it anyway. The row is gone; the count never saw it; **B's `comment_count` stays too high, permanently and silently.**

## Reachability

The write path cannot create this. `add_comment` validates that `reply_to` belongs to the same record, which is the guarantee `delete_comment(parent_id, comment_id)` also enforces. So it requires rows introduced outside the API — an import, a backfill, or hand-edited data.

That does **not** make it harmless: the corruption is silent, permanent, and lands on a record nobody touched.

## Why this is filed rather than fixed

Every option changes semantics of a transactional delete that already holds a lock on the parent row, and picking one is a design decision:

1. **Walk the closure record-agnostically, then maintain each affected record's counter.** Most correct, and the largest change: the closure must carry `commentable_id`, deltas become per-record, and the function currently locks and updates exactly one parent. Multi-record counter maintenance inside that lock needs its own thought about ordering and deadlocks.
2. **`ON DELETE RESTRICT` instead of `CASCADE` in the generated migration.** Nearly free, and converts silence into a loud FK violation. The app's own deletes are unaffected (the closure already contains every same-record descendant, and FK checks resolve at statement end). But it also makes the `#[commentable]` parent-delete trigger fail on corrupt data, and it only helps projects generated after the change.
3. **Recompute rather than delta.** Reuses the existing `recompute_comment_count`, but still needs to know which other records were touched — which is option 1's closure.

My inclination is 2 as an immediate guard plus 1 as the real fix, but that is worth a maintainer's call rather than a late-review commit.

## Note on severity

I have been fixing silent-breakage findings in this PR rather than filing them, on the principle that a loud failure can wait and a silent one cannot. This is a deliberate exception: the precondition is data the API cannot produce, and the delete path is transactional and lock-holding, so a careless fix here risks a worse bug than the one it closes.

## Test to write with the fix

Seed a comment on record A, a reply on record B whose `parent_id` points into A's subtree, hard-delete A's comment, then assert **both** records' `comment_count` match `SELECT count(*)` for their own rows.

records.title: CRITICAL: Sandbox filesystem on the mounted volume has a seriously degraded performance when created with DOCKER_SANDBOXES_ENABLE_VIRTIOFS_CACHE=1
records.body:
I found a critical FS performance degradation that popped up in a very recent release, most likely since the DOCKER_SANDBOXES_ENABLE_VIRTIOFS_CACHE=1 default value.

This prevents many common flows from working normally, such as npm installs or anything that performs large mutations on a lot of files and folders - even a plain rm -rf command.

I let my agent debug and reproduce the problem using a simple flow on 2 created sandboxes, one with the cache enabled and one without.


**My agent's full generated report:**

Summary
In this sandbox, a repo mounted under /Users/... is exposed inside the guest VM via virtiofs.

With the default cache-enabled mounted workspace, Node package-manager operations that need to delete or replace some existing directories inside node_modules can become pathologically slow on that mounted filesystem, to the point of appearing hung for long periods.

Important nuance: this behavior is selective, not universal. Some files or package directories may delete successfully, while others become extremely slow. The reproduction below uses a path that repeatedly behaved this way in this session.

This is not project-specific:

it reproduces with a minimal package.json containing only typescript
it reproduces with plain rm -rf, not just npm
the same commands succeed immediately on /tmp in the same session, with the same user, same Node, same npm, same network
Subsequent retesting on a similar sandbox created with DOCKER_SANDBOXES_ENABLE_VIRTIOFS_CACHE=0 removed the slowdown for both npm-driven and plain filesystem-mutation workloads, indicating that virtiofs caching is the decisive variable in this environment.

Environment observed in this session
mounted workspace path: /Users/omergilad/workspace/...
mount info:
bind-4e58314716db6303 on /Users/omergilad/workspace type virtiofs (rw,relatime)
comparison path: /tmp
Node: v22.22.1
npm: 11.17.0
Minimal reproduction
1) Create a minimal project on the mounted workspace
```
mkdir -p /Users/omergilad/workspace/go/virtiofs-repro-min
cat > /Users/omergilad/workspace/go/virtiofs-repro-min/package.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "virtiofs-repro-min",
  "private": true,
  "devDependencies": {
    "typescript": "5.9.3"
  }
}
EOF
npm --prefix /Users/omergilad/workspace/go/virtiofs-repro-min install --no-audit --no-fund
```
Observed result in this session:

added 1 package in 2s
So initial install succeeds on virtiofs.

2) Try to delete the installed package directory on the mounted workspace
```
timeout 5 rm -rf /Users/omergilad/workspace/go/virtiofs-repro-min/node_modules/typescript
printf 'exit=%s\n' "$?"
```
Observed result in this session:

exit=124
124 is timeout killing a command that had still not completed after 5 seconds.

This does not mean every rm -rf inside node_modules fails forever. In this session, some entries were removable while others were not; and for at least one such tree, a later unrestricted rm -rf eventually completed but took 85.10s. The key point is that recursive deletion on the mounted workspace is unreliable and path-dependent, and can be so slow that it looks hung.

3) Run the exact same reproduction on /tmp
```
mkdir -p /tmp/virtiofs-repro-min
cat > /tmp/virtiofs-repro-min/package.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "virtiofs-repro-min",
  "private": true,
  "devDependencies": {
    "typescript": "5.9.3"
  }
}
EOF
npm --prefix /tmp/virtiofs-repro-min install --no-audit --no-fund
npm --prefix /tmp/virtiofs-repro-min ci --no-audit --no-fund
timeout 5 rm -rf /tmp/virtiofs-repro-min/node_modules/typescript
printf 'exit=%s\n' "$?"
```
Observed result in this session:

added 1 package in 388ms
added 1 package in 304ms
exit=0
So the same dependency tree, under the same Node/npm, works correctly on /tmp.

Stronger npm-specific reproduction
On the mounted virtiofs path, after the first successful install:
`
npm --prefix /Users/omergilad/workspace/go/virtiofs-repro-min ci --no-audit --no-fund`
This had not completed within the observation window and was manually interrupted.

At the same time, the stuck npm process showed libuv worker threads blocked in filesystem delete syscalls:

PID     TID   STAT WCHAN              COMMAND
83455   83462 Dl+  filename_unlinkat  libuv-worker
83455   83463 Dl+  filename_unlinkat  libuv-worker
83455   83465 Dl+  filename_unlinkat  libuv-worker
The process also had an active io_uring fd open:

... [io_uring] ...
This strongly suggests the hang is in the mounted filesystem / guest filesystem stack, not in application logic.

Bottleneck characterization
The slow path is specifically filesystem mutation, not general traversal or dependency resolution.

Metadata reads are slower, but not enough to explain the problem
For the installed typescript tree (about 163 visible paths):

mounted virtiofs:
os.walk(...): about 0.0089s
lstat on every entry: about 0.0041s
/tmp:
os.walk(...): about 0.00024s
lstat on every entry: about 0.00046s
So read-only metadata operations are slower on virtiofs, but only by milliseconds here.

D
